questions.prompt: Is there a defect in how this code uses atomic operations and memory ordering? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
Many threads call ticket_create concurrently on the same pool. What does the memory_order_relaxed fetch_add on next_id guarantee?
choices: Each ticket gets a unique id, but the operation does not order surrounding reads and writes relative to other threads
Ids are handed out in the order in which the threads started the call
Ids are unique only if the pool is not closing
Ids are unique only when the surrounding code holds a mutex

questions.prompt: pool_try_reserve_slot uses a compare-exchange loop. Two threads race for the last free slot (queued == max_queued - 1). What happens?
choices: Both succeed, and queued exceeds max_queued by one
Both fail, because compare-exchange fails for concurrent callers
One succeeds; the other's compare-exchange fails, reloads current into the local variable, sees the limit reached, and returns false
One succeeds; the other spins until a slot is released and then succeeds

questions.prompt: ticket_retain increments refs with memory_order_relaxed. Under which usage is that acceptable?
choices: Only when called from the thread that created the ticket
Whenever the caller already owns a reference, because the count cannot reach zero during the increment and the increment needs no ordering for data the caller can already see
Whenever the ticket was found through a lock-free lookup by id, even if no reference is owned yet
Never; every atomic increment needs release semantics
